The resulting stress-strain curve provides invaluable insights into the material's mechanical properties, including its elastic limit, yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and Young's modulus. Stakeholders are keenly interested in understanding the intricate relationships between these material properties and the stress-strain curve. To address this, researchers turned to AI and ML to predict stress-strain curves of AM parts based on known metal properties. This innovative work was undertaken by Sharmistha Chakrabarti and Natan Debardeleben from the High Performance Computing and Design group at LANL, with their findings presented in this section. Following the preprocessing of the dataset, an in-depth exploratory data analysis was conducted to uncover hidden patterns and trends. The results of this analysis are visually represented in Figure 36, comprising four bar plots that illustrate the distribution percentages of various factors influencing the specimens. The first plot (Figure 36a) reveals that a significant majority, approximately 60%, of the specimens were manufactured by PAC, while the remaining 40% were produced by Praxair. The build direction, as shown in Figure 36b, has a notable impact, with around 69% of the specimens being fabricated vertically and 31% horizontally. Furthermore, Figure 36c indicates that only a small proportion, about 22%, of the specimens underwent heat treatment after fabrication.
